rationale: CRC is linked to a small group of oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas). Each one is sparse and low in abundance, so a random forest has trouble picking up the signal from any single genus. This change pools them into two taxonomy-name features: a mean log-abundance marker score and a count of how many marker genera are present. Both are added alongside the existing genus abundances and should transfer to other studies, since they use genus names rather than study-specific OTU ids.

Instead of a random forest on relative abundances, I'll switch to a centered log-ratio (CLR) transform on genus counts. CLR is the standard way to handle compositional data and depth variation. Before the transform, I'll drop genera present in under 10% of training samples, then train a standardized L2 logistic regression whose regularization strength is picked by grouped inner CV. This follows the SIAMCAT-style approach, where log-abundance linear models match or beat random forests for CRC. The hypothesis is that CRC signal is spread thinly across many log-scale genus shifts, which a regularized linear model captures better than random-forest splits on raw proportions.

The baseline lumps every OTU without a genus name into one `g__` column. In Baxter V4 data, that column mixes large unrelated groups (unclassified Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Enterobacteriaceae and others), so it mostly adds noise. This change keys each feature on its full lineage, so an unclassified genus becomes "deepest named rank + unclassified". It also adds family, order, class and phylum totals, which gives the random forest stable higher-level signals (such as Fusobacteriaceae/Porphyromonadaceae gains and Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae loss) that apply across studies by taxonomy name.

Many genera in Baxter V4 appear in only a few samples. Because the random forest tries a random √p subset of features at each split, these rare, near-constant genera fill most of the candidate slots and push out the informative ones. My hypothesis is that keeping only genera present in at least 10% of training-fold samples (filter learned on the training fold only) will focus splits on real CRC shifts and raise AUROC. The filter uses taxonomy names, so it should still transfer to other studies.

The CRC signal in Baxter mostly comes from a few sparse oral-pathogen genera, which are rare (that is likely why prevalence filtering hurt in round 4). A default RF only tries √p ≈ 14 genera per split, so it seldom gets to split on those few genera, and fully grown trees give noisy probability rankings on about 230 samples. This change picks the features tried per split (`max_features`) and minimum leaf size (`min_samples_leaf`) by grouped inner CV on the training fold, then refits a bigger forest (1000 trees) with the chosen settings. The features stay the same: genus names, so the model still transfers across studies.

Switch the random forest to an ExtraTrees forest (1000 trees) on log10 genus relative abundance, with a pseudocount of 1e-6. ExtraTrees draws split thresholds uniformly between each feature's min and max. On raw proportions those thresholds would almost never separate "absent" from "present at low abundance", and that is exactly the signal carried by sparse CRC oral pathogens like Fusobacterium, Parvimonas and Peptostreptococcus. On a log scale the thresholds spread across orders of magnitude, and the extra randomization should give smoother probability rankings than fully grown RF trees on about 230 samples.

Sequencing depth varies a lot across Baxter samples, so whether a sparse CRC genus (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas) is detected at all depends partly on read count rather than biology. That depth artifact is exactly what random-forest splits on "absent vs. present" pick up. This change rarefies each sample's genus counts to a common depth before computing relative abundances, using a fixed-seed draw without replacement at the 5th-percentile depth. That puts all samples on equal detection footing and removes depth-driven noise in rare-taxon presence. Because the rarefaction works on genus names, it should still transfer to other studies.

CRC stool tends to have shifted community diversity, and no earlier round has tested diversity measures. This change adds sample-level alpha-diversity features to the genus relative abundances used by the random forest. The features are OTU richness computed at one common depth with Hurlbert expected rarefaction (deterministic and fair across sequencing depths), plus Shannon, inverse Simpson, Pielou evenness and genus-level Shannon. None of them depend on study-specific OTU ids, so they should carry over to the other CRC studies.

Rather than adding marker features to the RF (round 1, which changed nothing), I'll build a separate small L2 logistic model on log abundances of the main CRC oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) and average its probabilities 50/50 with the unchanged genus RF. The idea is that the RF rarely splits on these sparse genera, while an additive log-scale model scores them directly. The two models should make different errors, so the blend should rank samples better. Both parts use genus names only, so the result should still transfer to other CRC studies.

The marker model only covers five oral pathogens. Meta-analyses (Wirbel 2019, Thomas 2019) report a wider group of oral anaerobes that are consistently enriched in CRC stool: Solobacterium, Peptoniphilus, Anaerococcus and Campylobacter. Each is sparse, so the random forest seldom splits on them, but together they add independent evidence that a sample comes from a CRC patient. Adding them to the L2 log-abundance logistic model should improve ranking. Everything stays keyed on genus names, so it still transfers to other studies.

The marker model currently adds a fixed 1e-5 pseudocount, so an absent oral pathogen gets the same value whether the sample had 5k reads or 100k reads. In reality, absence at high depth is much stronger evidence of a truly absent pathogen than absence at low depth. I replace the fixed pseudocount with a per-sample, depth-aware one of half a read (log10(rel + 0.5/depth)), so marker values reflect each sample's detection limit. The random forest part is unchanged.

The current blend averages raw probabilities from two models on very different scales. The RF's probabilities bunch together and often tie, while the logistic model's are spread out by the sigmoid, so whichever model has more spread controls the ranking. I'll turn each model's test score into a percentile against that model's own scores on the training samples, then average the percentiles. The RF uses its out-of-bag probabilities for this, so the reference isn't overfit, and the logistic model uses its training-set probabilities. Both models then count equally in a rank-based blend, which suits AUROC, and the scores stay comparable across folds and studies.

Raise the random forest from 500 to 2000 trees and change nothing else. With roughly 300 genera, each split looks at only about 17 random candidates, so the sparse CRC-informative genera get split on in few trees. With 500 trees, both the test probabilities and the OOB reference (each sample is OOB in only about 185 trees) are coarse and full of ties. More trees should make the RF ranking and its percentile calibration smoother and less noisy, which matters for a rank-based AUROC blend.

I'm replacing the fitted 5-coefficient marker logistic regression with a fixed, equal-weight score: the mean of training-standardized log10 abundances of the oral-pathogen markers. With about 120 cases, sparse and correlated markers, the fitted model can give noisy or even negative weights to markers we know are CRC-enriched. Fixing all weights to "enriched" should rank more robustly within Baxter and carry over better to the other CRC studies. The random forest and the percentile blend are unchanged.

The fixed marker score only measures the gain of oral pathogens. CRC stool also loses abundant butyrate producers (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia), and because those genera are abundant their measurement is much less affected by sequencing depth. This change folds them into the same equal-weight score with a negative sign, making it a signed log-ratio-like score of pathogens versus butyrate producers. The random forest and the percentile blend stay the same, and the score still uses genus names only, so it should transfer to the other studies.

The 50/50 percentile blend is a fixed guess, and how much the sparse oral-pathogen score should count relative to the genus RF depends on the data. This change picks the blend weight on each training fold by maximizing the training AUROC of the blend, using the RF's out-of-bag scores, which give an honest estimate without inner refits. The marker score has no fitted weights, so its training scores are also unbiased. The weight grid is limited to 0.2–0.8, and ties go to the value closest to 0.5, to avoid overfitting.

The marker score currently z-scores log10(rel + 1e-5) values. These markers are mostly zero, so the gap between "absent" and "detected" depends on an arbitrary pseudocount, and a few samples with heavy blooms inflate each marker's SD and shrink everyone else's contribution. I'll replace the z-score with each marker's mid-rank percentile within its training-fold distribution and average those percentiles. Each marker then weighs detection against abundance according to its own prevalence, and the result does not depend on the pseudocount or the scale.

Different tumours seem to carry different oral pathogens (Fusobacterium in some, Parvimonas or Porphyromonas in others). Averaging the five marker percentiles dilutes one strong bloom with the other markers' absence. I'm replacing the mean with Fisher's combination of each marker's upper-tail empirical p-value, so a single extreme marker can push a sample high. This keeps equal positive weights, stays rank-based and still uses genus names only.

Fisher's method assumes each p-value is computed under the null hypothesis, but the marker p-values are currently ranked against the whole training fold, which includes the CRC cases (about 40% of it). That makes pathogen blooms look less extreme than they are. I'll compute each marker's upper-tail empirical p-value against the healthy controls in the training fold only. Detecting a marker then counts as strong evidence when it is rare in healthy stool, and as weak evidence when it is common there (for example Gemella or Porphyromonas).

Every attempt to tune the genus RF itself has failed (rounds 4–7 and 13), so I'm leaving the RF as is and averaging it with a shallow, strongly regularized CatBoost model on the same genus abundances. Boosting fits the data sequentially and should catch additive genus shifts that bagged, fully grown trees miss, so the two models' errors should only partly overlap. The marker score still gets half the weight, and CatBoost's percentile reference comes from grouped inner-CV out-of-fold scores, so the calibration stays honest.
